extraction_text: King Janamejaya requests the sage Vaishampayana to explain how legitimate charity yields great merit, referencing the story of the gleaner who gained great merit by giving a handful of flour.
Vaishampayana begins narrating an ancient story about the great sage Agastya performing a twelve-year purification ritual (Mahayajna).
Many ascetic priests and sages, including Yatis and mendicants, attend Agastya's sacrifice, all characterized by purity, self-control, and adherence to dharma.
Indra, the king of gods, stops rainfall during Agastya's sacrifice, causing concern among the sages about the lack of food for the charity.
The sages discuss the dilemma: Agastya's twelve-year sacrifice requires food for charity, but Indra's withholding of rain for twelve years would prevent food production.

Agastya, hearing their concern, declares his resolve to continue the sacrifice regardless, vowing to use stored seeds, perform mental sacrifices, or even become Indra himself to ensure life's sustenance.

attributes.action: Asserting determination to overcome divine obstacle

extraction_text: Agastya commands all celestial beings, wealth from the northern continent (Uttarakuru), and even heaven itself to appear at his sacrifice, asserting his power to ensure its success.
The Munis (sages) saw the ascetic power of the Muni (sage) and spoke meaningful words expressing their satisfaction with their own sacrifices and desire to perform them lawfully.

attributes.relationships: Munis acknowledging the sage's power but maintaining their own path

extraction_text: The Munis stated they lawfully obtain food, adhere to duties, follow celibacy, study the Vedas, and after completing celibacy, leave home to practice asceticism as per Dharma.

The Munis affirmed the sage's view against killing as correct and urged him to always declare non-killing in sacrifices, which would please them, and they would leave the sacrificial ground once the sacrifice was completed.

attributes.relationships: Munis supporting the sage's anti-killing stance

extraction_text: Vaishampayana narrated that upon their words, Indra (the destroyer of cities, king of gods) saw the ascetic power of the Muni and began to rain.

attributes.relationships: Indra responding to the sage's power

extraction_text: Indra, without waiting for the sacrifice to end, showered abundant rain and, led by Brihaspati, personally came to appease Sage Aurva.

attributes.relationships: Indra and Brihaspati intervening to calm Sage Aurva

extraction_text: Upon completion of the sacrifice, Sage Aurva was extremely pleased, paid respects to the great Munis according to ritual, and bid them farewell.

attributes.relationships: Sage Aurva honoring the Munis at the sacrifice's end
